title: Running with injury: A study of UK novice and recreational runners and factors associated with running related injury
journal: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
population: UK parkrun runners who completed a web survey (novice and recreational)
findings: Retrospective cross-sectional web survey of 1145 respondents; 570 had a current injury and 86% kept running despite pain.
In the first year of running, runners using a self-devised training programme were more likely to be injured than those using a structured programme such as Couch to 5K.

Running experience of over 2 years was protective (OR 0.578-0.65); males were 1.45 times more likely to be injured; wearing orthotics OR 1.88; lack of previous injuries in the past 12 months OR 1.44 (as printed in the abstract, an unexplained direction).
Authors: a novice runner should use a recognised structured training programme; graduated loading is important for novices.
limitations: Retrospective, self-selected, self-reported, cross-sectional (cannot show cause); structured plans were not compared with each other or with continuous 3 x 20; one reported association (no prior injury OR 1.44) is counter-intuitive.
implications: Supports giving a novice a structured, graded plan rather than leaving the first weeks unplanned, at grade C.
Experience of over 2 years is a candidate threshold for treating a returner as experienced; below that, keep a gentler start.
Supports a structured, graded Couch-to-5K-style start for new runners rather than a free-form first block.
Engine inference, not stated in the source: in the first year a new runner's long run is better set as a gradual extension of the longest recent continuous run than as a share-of-week target.
